title: Solar Company Website Cost: What You'll Actually Pay in 2026
description: A solar company website costs $3,000 to $25,000 depending on features and customization. Here's what you actually need to turn visitors into booked installs.
keywords: solar company website cost, website for solar companies, solar installer website price, how much does a solar website cost
author: Abdulrehman Saghir
contentHtml:
A professional website for a solar installation company costs between $3,000 and $25,000 in 2026. Template-based sites run $2,000 to $8,000, custom-designed sites with lead generation features cost $8,000 to $25,000, and enterprise solutions with advanced integrations start at $25,000. Most solar companies need five things: a clear homepage that names the outcome, proof of real installs, mobile-ready design, a booking system, and basic SEO — everything else is optional until you have steady leads.

What drives the cost of a solar company website?

The price depends on three factors: customization level, features included, and build timeline.

Template-based websites ($2,000–$8,000) use pre-designed themes customized with your branding and content. You get basic pages, a contact form, and limited customization. These deploy in 2–4 weeks but look like templates — which matters when a homeowner is choosing who installs $30,000 worth of solar panels on their roof.

Custom-designed websites ($8,000–$25,000) are built from scratch around your brand and the solar buying journey. They include conversion features like solar savings calculators, financing information, project galleries, local SEO optimization, and CRM integration. Build time is typically 6–12 weeks with a traditional agency.

Enterprise solutions ($25,000–$100,000+) are for multi-location solar companies that need customer portals, real-time monitoring dashboards, inventory systems, and complex integrations. Unless you're running 10+ locations or managing hundreds of installs simultaneously, you don't need this tier.

The cost gap between template and custom isn't about aesthetics — it's about conversion infrastructure. A template gives you a digital brochure. A custom build gives you a lead generation system.

What features does a solar company website actually need?

Most solar company websites are overbuilt or underbuilt. Here's what you need to turn visitors into booked installs, and what you can skip.

Must-have features (tier 1)

Outcome-focused homepage. Your homepage headline should name who you serve (solar installation companies or homeowners) and the result they get. "Solar Installation in Austin — Save Up to 90% on Electricity" beats "Powering a Brighter Tomorrow." Be specific. Be local. Be clear about the outcome.

Proof — real project photos. Homeowners spending $20,000 to $40,000 need to see you've done this before. A gallery of real installs — rooftop panels, ground mounts, finished projects — builds more trust than any testimonial. If you're just starting and don't have client work yet, show demo builds or training projects. Real beats stock photos every time.

Mobile-responsive design. Over 60% of solar searches happen on mobile. Your site must load fast (under 3 seconds), have a tap-to-call button on every page, and let someone request a quote without zooming or endless scrolling. Test it on an actual phone — if you can't find the call button in two taps, you're losing leads.

Booking system or quote form. The easier you make it to book, the more calls you get. A direct booking link (Calendly, Acuity) removes friction. If you prefer quote forms, keep them short — name, phone, address, monthly electric bill. Every extra field costs you conversions.

Basic local SEO setup. Your homepage needs your city and state in the main headline, your business name and phone number must match your Google Business Profile exactly, and your site needs to load fast with clean code. This is the foundation that helps you show up when someone searches "solar installer near me."

Worth adding once you have steady leads (tier 2)

Solar savings calculator. A calculator that estimates monthly savings based on a homeowner's electric bill is one of the highest-converting features in solar web design. It captures leads (name, email, phone required to see results) and pre-qualifies them based on bill size. A homeowner with a $400/month bill is a different prospect than one with a $100 bill.

Cost to add: $1,500–$5,000 depending on complexity.

Financing information page. Most homeowners finance solar. A clear page explaining loan options, lease terms, and incentives (federal tax credits, state rebates, net metering) answers the "how do I pay for this" question before they call. This doesn't require integration — just a well-written page.

Service area pages. If you serve multiple cities, each city needs its own page with local content: utility company details, average savings in that area, local permitting notes. These pages help you rank for "[city] solar installation" searches. One page per city, real local content — not just templates that swap the city name.

Skip until you're scaling (tier 3)

Customer portals. Real-time monitoring dashboards and customer login areas sound impressive but add $5,000–$15,000+ to the build and require ongoing maintenance. Unless you're managing 50+ active customers, you don't need this yet.

Live chat or chatbots. AI-powered chat assistants cost $3,000–$8,000 to set up and $100–$300/month to run. They work for high-traffic sites but add complexity for a solar company just starting out. A phone number and a quote form work fine until you're getting 50+ leads per month.

Advanced CRM integrations. Connecting your website to HubSpot, Salesforce, or Jobber can cost $2,000–$10,000+ depending on the system. Start with a simple Google Sheet or a lightweight CRM (like Airtable or Notion) until the volume justifies the cost.

The pattern: start with the features that turn a visitor into a call. Add complexity only when lead volume or operational pain justifies it.

How long does it take to build a solar company website?

A custom solar website typically takes 6 to 12 weeks with a traditional agency. Template-based sites are faster — 2 to 4 weeks — but sacrifice customization and conversion optimization.

The timeline breaks down into:

  • Discovery and planning (1–2 weeks): understanding your service area, competitors, and positioning
  • Design (2–4 weeks): wireframes, mockups, and revisions
  • Development (2–4 weeks): building the site, adding content, setting up forms and integrations
  • Testing and launch (1 week): mobile testing, speed optimization, SEO checks

Some agencies (like Lumen Web Studio) compress this to one week by working with a clear process, using modern tools, and building for solar companies specifically. Longer timelines usually mean back-and-forth revisions, waiting on content, or building custom features that aren't essential.

Ask before you commit: "What's the timeline from kickoff to live, and what would delay it?" The answer tells you whether the agency has a process or is guessing.

Template vs. custom: which one should you choose?

Here's the real difference between a $3,000 template site and a $15,000 custom build:

| | Template Site | Custom Build | |---|---|---| | Design | Looks like other template sites | Unique to your brand | | Conversion paths | Generic contact form | Built around the solar buying journey | | Trust signals | Stock photos, generic "trust us" | Real install photos, certifications, local proof | | Local SEO | Basic or none | City pages, schema markup, local content | | Mobile | Responsive as an afterthought | Designed mobile-first for solar's mobile-heavy audience | | Speed | Often slow (bloated plugins, unoptimized images) | Clean code, fast load times | | Lead generation | Hope someone fills out the form | Designed to turn visitors into calls | | Timeline | 2–4 weeks | 6–12 weeks (or 1 week with the right agency) |

A template site works if you need something live fast and cheap, and you plan to replace it once you have revenue. A custom site works if you're treating your website as your primary lead generation tool and need it to perform, not just exist.

The decision isn't about budget — it's about whether your website is a placeholder or a profit center.

What does a solar company website actually cost?

Here's the honest breakdown for 2026:

| Tier | What You Get | Price Range | Timeline | |------|--------------|-------------|----------| | DIY / Template | Wix, Squarespace, or WordPress theme you customize yourself | $500–$2,000 | 1–2 weeks | | Freelancer / Template | Designer customizes a pre-built theme for you | $2,000–$8,000 | 2–4 weeks | | Custom / Small Agency | Built from scratch, conversion-focused, basic SEO | $8,000–$25,000 | 6–12 weeks | | Full-Service Agency | Custom design, advanced features, ongoing retainer | $25,000–$100,000+ | 12+ weeks |

Most solar installation companies fall into the $3,000–$15,000 range: custom enough to stand out, conversion-focused enough to generate leads, and fast enough to launch before the season ends.

Add-on costs to expect:

  • Hosting: $10–$100/month depending on traffic
  • Domain: $15–$50/year
  • SSL certificate: Often included, or $0–$100/year
  • Ongoing updates: $50–$500/month if you hire it out, or you can make small updates yourself

Retainers are optional. Some agencies charge $500–$2,000/month for updates, SEO, and support. Others (like us) build the site, hand you the keys, and charge only if you need help later. Ask upfront: "What happens after launch, and what does it cost?"

Is a solar company website worth the cost?

Here's the math that matters.

The average residential solar installation is $27,000 (NREL, 2024). At a 20% gross margin, that's $5,400 profit per job.

A $9,000 website that brings you one extra lead per month — at a 20% close rate — puts $12,960 in profit back in your pocket every year. That's a 1.4x return in year one, and year two is pure profit since the site is already paid for.

Break-even is one-fifth of one install. If your website generates even one lead per month that converts, you're in ROI within the first few weeks.

The question isn't what a website costs. It's what a website earns. A $3,000 site that generates zero leads is more expensive than a $15,000 site that books two jobs a month.

What makes a good solar company website?

A good solar website does three things:

  1. Loads fast. Under 3 seconds on mobile. Over 50% of visitors bounce if your site is slow. Uncompressed project photos and bloated WordPress plugins are the usual culprits.

  2. Answers the three questions every homeowner asks:

    • What will it cost?
    • How much will I save?
    • How do I get started?

  3. Makes it easy to take the next step. Every page has a clear call-to-action (CTA) — book a call, request a quote, calculate savings. The CTA button is visible, tappable on mobile, and uses low-stakes language like "free quote" or "30-minute call, no pressure."

Everything else — the fonts, the colors, the animations — is secondary. Speed, clarity, and a clear path to book are what turn visitors into customers.

How to choose a web designer for your solar company

Ask these five questions before you commit:

1. Have you built websites for solar companies before?

Solar is different from general contracting. Homeowners research for weeks, compare multiple installers, and need specific information: financing options, federal tax credits, savings projections, and proof you're licensed and insured. A designer who understands the solar buying journey builds a better site than one who treats it like any other service business.

2. What's the timeline from kickoff to live?

If they say "8–12 weeks," ask what drives that. Is it design revisions? Waiting on content? Building custom features? A clear process compresses timelines. Some agencies deliver in a week. Others take three months. Know what you're signing up for.

3. What happens after launch?

Some agencies require ongoing retainers ($500–$2,000/month). Others hand you the keys and charge only for future updates. Neither is wrong, but know the cost before you commit. Ask: "If I want to update a page or add a new service six months from now, what does that cost?"

4. Will I be able to update the site myself?

Some sites are locked to the agency — you need them for every change. Others are built on platforms (WordPress, Webflow) where you can edit text and images yourself. If you want control, ask upfront.

5. What does SEO setup include?

"SEO included" means different things to different agencies. At minimum, you need: fast page speed, mobile-responsive design, proper heading structure, meta titles and descriptions, local business schema markup, and your city in the homepage headline. Ask what's included and what costs extra.

Do you need a website if you're just starting a solar company?

Yes — but maybe not the $15,000 version yet.

If you're pre-revenue or getting your first few customers from door-knocking and referrals, start with a simple 3–5 page site: homepage, services, proof (even if it's training installs), process, and contact. Budget: $3,000–$6,000. Get it live, use it to close the customers you're already talking to, and upgrade once you have steady revenue.

If you're already booking installs and turning away leads, a $10,000–$15,000 custom site with conversion features (calculator, local SEO, service area pages) pays for itself in one or two jobs.

The mistake is either waiting too long (losing credibility and leads) or overbuilding too early (spending $25,000 before you know what converts). Match the site to the stage you're in.

Frequently asked questions

How much does a website cost for a solar company?

A professional solar company website costs $3,000 to $25,000 depending on customization and features. Template-based sites are $2,000–$8,000, custom builds are $8,000–$25,000, and enterprise solutions start at $25,000. Most solar companies spend $8,000–$15,000 for a custom, conversion-focused site.

Can I build a solar website myself?

Yes, using platforms like Wix, Squarespace, or WordPress. Budget $500–$2,000 for the theme, domain, and hosting. The tradeoff: you'll spend 20–40 hours building it, it'll look like a template, and you'll miss conversion features (local SEO, lead capture optimization, speed tuning) that a professional build includes. DIY works if you're pre-revenue and need something live fast.

How long does a solar website last before I need to redesign?

A well-built solar website lasts 3–5 years before needing a redesign. Plan for minor updates (new projects, updated financing info, pricing changes) every 6–12 months. Technology, design trends, and Google's ranking factors change, so a full refresh every 3–5 years keeps your site competitive.

Do I need a blog on my solar website?

Not at launch. A blog helps with SEO — ranking for long-tail searches like "how much do solar panels cost in [city]" or "are solar panels worth it in [state]" — but only if you publish consistently (2–4 posts per month). Start with a strong 5-page site. Add a blog once you have time to maintain it or hire someone to write for you.

What's the ROI of a solar company website?

A $9,000 website that generates one extra lead per month pays for itself in under a year. At $27,000 average install value and 20% gross margin, one lead per month at a 20% close rate returns $12,960 in profit annually. Break-even is one-fifth of one install. If your website books even one job, you're in ROI within weeks.

Ready to turn your website into a lead generation system?

Most solar companies treat their website like a business card — something that just needs to exist. The ones winning treat it like their best salesperson: always on, always ready to close, and getting better with every lead.

contentHtml:
Solar Website Design for Installation Companies

Your solar website should do one thing: get the phone to ring. Not look pretty. Not win design awards. Generate booked installs.

Most solar company websites fail at this. They're digital brochures — a logo, a list of services, maybe a contact form buried at the bottom. Visitors land, glance, and leave. No calls. No quotes. No jobs.

Solar website design that actually works is different. It answers the three questions every homeowner asks before they pick up the phone: What will it cost? How much will I save? How do I get started? Then it gives them one clear path to book.

Here's what separates a solar website that converts from one that just exists.

Why Most Solar Websites Don't Generate Leads

The average solar installer's website has three problems.

It's a template, not a strategy. A Wix or Squarespace template gives you a pretty page. It doesn't give you conversion paths, trust signals, or a layout designed around how homeowners actually research solar. You're paying $500 for something that generates $0.

It loads too slow. Over 70% of solar website traffic is mobile. If your site takes more than 3 seconds to load on a phone, more than half your visitors bounce before they read a word. Uncompressed project photos and bloated plugins are the usual culprits.

It doesn't answer the buyer's questions. A homeowner considering solar spends weeks researching. They want to know if their roof is a fit, what the incentives are in their state, and what other homeowners in their area paid. If your site doesn't answer these questions, they'll find a competitor's site that does.

The result? You're paying for traffic — through ads, referrals, or door-knocking — and your website is leaking it. Every visitor who leaves without calling is a $27,000 install walking to your competitor.

The 5 Features Every Solar Website Needs to Convert

1. A Conversion-Focused Hero Section

Your hero section has 3 seconds to answer: What do you do? Who is it for? Why should I trust you?

A strong solar website hero includes:

  • One clear headline with your service and location (e.g., "Solar Installation in Austin, TX — Save Up to 90% on Electricity")
  • One subheadline stating your strongest homeowner benefit
  • One CTA button visible without scrolling — "Get a Free Quote" or "See Your Savings"
  • Trust indicators immediately below — years in business, panels installed, certifications

Skip the vague taglines like "Powering a Brighter Tomorrow." Be specific. Be local. Be clear.

2. Trust Signals Above the Fold

Solar is a high-consideration purchase. Homeowners are spending $15,000 to $40,000. They need to believe you're legitimate before they'll call.

Place these trust signals where they're impossible to miss:

  • Certifications: NABCEP badge, manufacturer partner logos (SunPower, Tesla, Enphase)
  • Review count and star rating: A live Google Reviews widget showing your actual rating
  • Local proof: "Over 200 homes powered in [Your City]" beats any tagline
  • Insurance and licensing: Display your contractor license number clearly

The installers converting best stack multiple trust signals near the point of decision — not buried in a footer, not on a separate "About" page. Right next to the CTA.

3. A Solar Savings Calculator

A savings calculator is one of the highest-converting features in solar web design. It gives homeowners a personalized result in exchange for their contact information.

How it works:

  • Simple inputs: Monthly electric bill, ZIP code, homeownership status
  • Instant output: Estimated monthly and annual savings
  • Lead capture: Name, email, phone required before showing results
  • Visual result: Before-solar bill vs. after-solar bill comparison

The calculator does three things simultaneously: educates the homeowner, captures a qualified lead, and pre-qualifies them based on their bill amount. A homeowner with a $400/month bill is a different prospect than one with a $120 bill.

4. Mobile-First Responsive Design

More people search for solar installers on their phones than on desktops. Your website must work flawlessly on mobile:

  • Click-to-call button large and tappable on every page
  • Simple navigation with 5 items or fewer
  • Condensed content that delivers the most important information without endless scrolling
  • Optimized forms with large touch-friendly fields and auto-fill

Test your site on an actual phone right now. Can you tap the call button without zooming? Can you find your services in two taps? If not, you're losing leads.

5. Local SEO Architecture

A beautiful solar website that doesn't rank locally is an expensive digital brochure. Local SEO must be built into your site from the start:

  • Location keyword in the homepage H1 (e.g., "Solar Company in Phoenix, AZ")
  • NAP consistency: Your name, address, and phone must match your Google Business Profile exactly
  • City landing pages: One unique, content-rich page for every city you serve
  • Schema markup: LocalBusiness structured data that helps Google understand your business
  • Embedded Google Map on your contact page

Each city page needs genuine local content — local permitting details, utility company information, average savings for that area. Templated pages that just swap the city name get penalized by Google.

Solar Website Design vs. Generic Templates

Here's the real difference between a custom solar website and a $500 template:

| | Custom Solar Website | Generic Template | |---|---|---| | Conversion paths | Built around the solar buying journey | Generic contact form | | Trust signals | Solar-specific (NABCEP, install photos, reviews) | Generic "trust us" | | Local SEO | City pages, schema, local content | None | | Mobile optimization | Designed for solar's mobile-first audience | Responsive as an afterthought | | Speed | Clean code, optimized images | Bloated plugins, slow load | | Result | Leads, calls, booked installs | A nice-looking brochure |

A template website looks fine. It just doesn't work. When you're competing against companies with bigger marketing budgets, your website can't be the weak link.

What Solar Website Design Costs in 2026

Solar website design pricing ranges based on complexity:

| Tier | What You Get | Price Range | |------|-------------|-------------| | Freelancer / Template | Basic site, no strategy, no SEO | $250–$1,500 | | Small Agency | Custom design, basic SEO, 5–8 pages | $2,500–$10,000 | | Full-Service Agency | Custom design, SEO, content, ongoing retainer | $10,000–$50,000+ |

The question isn't what a website costs. It's what a website earns.

Here's the math. The average residential solar install is $27,000 (NREL 2024). At 20% gross margin, that's $5,400 in profit per job. A $900 website that brings you one extra lead per month — at just a 20% close rate — puts $12,960 in profit back in your pocket every year.

That's a 14× return on a one-time investment.

The website pays for itself with one-fifth of one install. If it generates even one lead per month that converts, you're in ROI within the first week.

Local SEO: Why Your Solar Website Must Rank

Most homeowners start their solar research with a Google search: "solar installer near me," "solar company in [city]," "how much do solar panels cost in [state]."

If your website doesn't show up for these searches, those leads go to whoever does.

The foundation:

  • Google Business Profile: Fully optimized with 50+ photos, weekly posts, and accurate service areas. This is the most powerful local SEO asset you have, and it's free.
  • City service pages: One page per city you serve, with unique local content about permits, utilities, and savings in that area.
  • Review velocity: Collect 3–5 Google reviews per month minimum. Installers with 100+ reviews and a 4.8+ average consistently outrank competitors with fewer reviews.
  • Technical SEO: Fast load speed (under 3 seconds), HTTPS security, proper heading hierarchy, and schema markup.

Local SEO takes 6–12 months to build meaningful rankings, but the economics at maturity are better than any paid channel: cost per lead drops to $15–$40, close rates hit 20–28%, and every lead is exclusively yours.

The installers getting it right aren't doing anything exotic. They're just not cutting the corners that feel harmless individually but compound into a site that neither ranks nor converts.

Frequently Asked Questions About Solar Website Design

How much does a solar website cost? Solar website design ranges from $250 for a basic template site to $50,000+ for a full-service agency build. Most conversion-focused solar websites fall in the $900–$10,000 range. The key is ROI — a $900 website that generates one extra lead per month pays for itself 14× over in the first year.

What makes a good solar website? A good solar website loads fast (under 3 seconds), works perfectly on mobile, shows trust signals above the fold (certifications, reviews, install count), includes a savings calculator, and has clear CTAs on every page. It answers the three questions every homeowner asks: What will it cost? How much will I save? How do I get started?

Do I need separate pages for each service? Yes. Each service — residential solar, commercial solar, battery storage, solar financing — needs its own page to rank on Google and convert visitors searching for that specific service. One generic "Services" page won't rank for individual service searches.

How long does it take to build a solar website? A custom solar website typically takes 2–5 weeks. Some agencies (like Lumen Web Studio) can deliver a conversion-focused site in 7 days. Template-based sites are faster but don't include strategy, SEO, or conversion optimization.

Should I use WordPress or a custom build? For solar companies, a custom-built site (React, Next.js, or similar) outperforms WordPress in speed and SEO. WordPress themes inject unnecessary code that slows load times. A lean, custom-coded site loads faster, ranks better, and converts more visitors.

Ready to Turn Your Website Into a Lead Machine?

Your website is the most important lead generation asset your company has. Every channel — SEO, ads, social media, referrals — sends traffic there first. A weak website makes every upstream channel underperform.
